reconstructed_theorem_text:
For every natural number n, let E = R^n with its standard Euclidean norm and real inner product, and let S = {zeta in E : ||zeta|| = 1}. Let tau be the unnormalized polar measure on S induced by n-dimensional Lebesgue volume: for measurable A contained in S, tau(A) is n times the Lebesgue volume of {t zeta : 0 < t < 1, zeta in A}; for n = 0, tau is the zero measure. For every function F : E -> E, center a in E, and real radius R > 0, suppose F is locally continuously real differentiable of order one at every point of the closed ball K = {x in E : ||x-a|| <= R}. Define div F(x) as the sum, over the n standard coordinates i, of the directional derivative of the coordinate function F_i at x in the standard coordinate direction e_i. Then div F belongs to L1 of Lebesgue volume restricted to the open ball B = {x in E : ||x-a|| < R}; the scalar function zeta -> <F(a + R zeta), zeta> belongs to L1(S,tau); and the real Bochner integrals satisfy
integral_B div F(x) dx = R^(n-1) integral_S <F(a + R zeta), zeta> d tau(zeta).
The subtraction n-1 in the exponent is natural-number subtraction, truncated at zero. The statement includes dimensions n = 0 and n = 1, so the exponent equals zero in both cases, and in dimension zero the sum defining div F is empty and tau is zero. The two L1 assertions are conclusions in addition to the integral equality.
objects: The Euclidean space E = R^n; a vector field F : E -> E; a center a; a positive radius R; the open ball B(a,R), closed ball K = closedBall(a,R), and unit-sphere subtype S; Lebesgue volume on E; its unnormalized polar measure tau on S; the actual coordinate divergence div F; and the scalar radial component zeta -> <F(a+R zeta),zeta>.
domains: n ranges over all natural numbers, including 0 and 1; E has the standard real l2 norm and inner product; F is defined on all of E; a belongs to E; R is real and positive; the interior integral and its L1 assertion use Lebesgue volume restricted to the open ball ||x-a|| < R; local C1 regularity is assumed at every point of the closed ball ||x-a|| <= R; the sphere integral and its L1 assertion use tau on S = {zeta : ||zeta|| = 1}. For measurable A in S, tau(A) = n times volume({t zeta : 0 < t < 1, zeta in A}); tau is zero when n = 0.
quantifiers: For every n in N, every F : E -> E, every a in E, every R in R with 0 < R, and every instance of the hypothesis that F is locally C1 at all x in closedBall(a,R), all three conclusions hold. There is no existentially selected vector field, divergence, measure, or constant.
assumptions: R > 0. At each x in closedBall(a,R), F is actually continuously real differentiable of order one on a neighborhood of x. There is no restriction n >= 1 or n >= 2 and no separately supplied divergence certificate.
conclusion: The actual coordinate divergence, namely the finite sum of the derivative of F_i along e_i, is L1 for Lebesgue volume restricted to ball(a,R). The scalar function zeta -> <F(a+R zeta),zeta> is L1 for tau. Moreover integral_{ball(a,R)} div F(x) dx = R^(n-1) times integral_S <F(a+R zeta),zeta> d tau(zeta), with real Bochner integrals. These L1 conclusions are additional assertions, not consequences inferred solely from a displayed integral equality.
scopes: The C1 hypothesis is pointwise local on neighborhoods of all points of the closed ball, including its boundary. The divergence is integrated only over the open ball. The boundary radial component is evaluated at a+R zeta but integrated on the unit sphere using tau, with the displayed factor R^(n-1). The subtraction in n-1 is truncated natural subtraction; its value is zero for n = 0 and n = 1. Dimension zero is included, with empty coordinate sum and zero tau. Both L1 assertions and the equality lie under the same universal choices and assumptions.
constant_dependencies: There are no existential constants or unspecified estimates. The measure tau is determined by n and standard Lebesgue volume. The explicit factor R^(n-1) depends only on n and R; it is 1 for n = 0 and n = 1. The asserted integrability and identity are for the universally chosen F, a, and R.
